title: B.C. shooting victim was suicidal
subtitle: A young man shot by the RCMP in British Columbia after brandishing a knife on Thursday was threatening to kill himself, police said Friday
article: A young man shot by the RCMP in British Columbia after brandishing a knife on Thursday was threatening to kill himself, police said Friday.
Family members identified Chris Klim, 23, as the man killed by officers in the B.C. Interior city of Vernon when they went to execute a warrant under the Mental Health Act.
According to friends and family members, Mr. Klim suffered from mental health problems and was refusing to take his medication.
"Everyone wished that the outcome had been better. No one wanted this outcome. Not us, not the police, not anyone wanted this outcome," said Shirley Klim, his grandmother.
Shirley said she and her husband, Harry Klim, had looked after Chris for years, and that he suffered from some mental health issues that she didn't specify.
On Friday RCMP spokeswoman Const. Cathy Scott said officers went to Mr. Klim's apartment after learning he was suicidal.

"Police attempted to make phone contact with the male and could hear the phone inside the apartment, however, there was no answer. Out of concern for his safety, the decision was made to use force to gain entry to the apartment," Scott said in a written statement. When officers entered, they found Mr. Klim holding a knife.

"They tried talking to him but he refused to drop the knife. The (Taser) was then deployed and only had a momentary effect on the male. He again advanced on the members inside the apartment with the knife. He continued to disobey the verbal commands to drop the knife, which resulted in deadly force being used."
Mr. Klim was taken to hospital, where he died.
The RCMP's major crime section is investigating, as is the B.C. Coroners Service and the Commission for Public Complaints against the RCMP.
Mary-Kathryn Albrecht, who lived in the same apartment building, said she would often encounter Mr. Klim in the foyer and he would talk to her.
She said he was a sweet person who lived alone and was on social assistance. But in recent weeks he had become increasingly disturbed and had told her he didn't want to take his medications anymore.

"I know he was upset over being made to take his injections and his medication, and he had said a couple of times when I ran into him last week, 'I never hurt anybody, I never hurt anybody,' " Ms. Albrecht said.
His distress apparently hit a high point during the holidays, she said.
"I know he had some friends, but he said the week before Christmas that they were doing their own thing and his family didn't want too much to do with him."

Shirley Klim said her family was still trying to deal with the tragedy and was awaiting the outcome of the police investigation. She said her grandson was estranged from his father, and she and her husband were his main support.
His father, Clarence Klim, said he knew his son was having problems, but didn't keep in contact.
"He just didn't want to take the medication, and he felt he didn't need it," he said. "He tried to kill himself a few years ago, and he would get depressed lots."
He last saw his son about two months ago and only learned of the shooting Friday morning.
The incident is one of several police shootings in Western Canada this week involving people brandishing knives, including a pair of shootings in Saskatoon.
Last Saturday, a Saskatoon police officer shot and killed 38-year-old Dwayne Charles Dustyhorn.
According to police, Mr. Dustyhorn was armed with two knives, including one strapped to his wrist, and charged officers in a basement apartment.
Then, on Thursday, Saskatoon police shot a woman in the chest who witnesses said had been wielding a knife in each hand.
The woman remained in hospital in serious but stable condition Friday, and police said she may face weapons charges.
